stem: Hayes’s promise of “local self-government” for the South most directly signaled

options.text: a new federal program to protect Black voting rights
the admission of new Southern states to the Union
options.misconception: New Southern states were at issue.

options.text: a plan to divide the South into federal military districts
the end of federal intervention in Southern politics

rationales.A: Promising local rule points away from federal protection, not toward it.
rationales.B: The Southern states were already in the Union; no new states were at issue.
rationales.C: Military districts belonged to Reconstruction, the system Hayes was ending.
rationales.D: Background: “local self-government” meant rule by Southerners themselves, without federal troops and officials, and Hayes’s inaugural came days after the Compromise of 1877 settled the disputed election in his favor; the last federal troops left the South the following month, in April 1877.
rationales.general:
1. Read the promise. “Local self-government” as the South’s own resource.
2. Ask what local rule replaces. Background: federal troops and Reconstruction governments, which the Compromise of 1877 was removing.
3. Test the other readings. No new protection, no new states, and no new military rule fit the words.
4. Match the signal. Hayes was announcing that Washington would step back and let the South govern itself.
Remember: “local self-government” is a promise about who rules — ask who steps back when it is kept.

stimulus.source_note: Rutherford B. Hayes, Inaugural Address, March 5, 1877. Public domain.
stimulus.text:
“I am sincerely anxious to use every legitimate influence in favor of honest and efficient local self-government as the true resource of those States for the promotion of the contentment and prosperity of their citizens. . . .

Let me assure my countrymen of the Southern States that it is my earnest desire to regard and promote their truest interest — the interests of the white and of the colored people both and equally — and to put forth my best efforts in behalf of a civil policy which will forever wipe out in our political affairs the color line and the distinction between North and South, to the end that we may have not merely a united North or a united South, but a united country.”

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain inaugural address
